[[File:Sauge sclarée.jpg|thumb|Sauge sclarée in "Les plantes potagères" Vilmorin 1925]]
'''''Salvia sclarea''''', the '''clary''' or '''clary sage''' (clary deriving from [[Middle English]] ''clarie'', from [[Anglo-Norman language|Anglo-Norman]] ''sclaree'', from [[Late Latin|Late]] or [[Medieval Latin]] ''[[wikt:sclareia|sclarēia]]'' meaning ''clear''), is a [[Biennial plant|biennial]] (short-lived) herbaceous [[perennial]] in the genus ''[[Salvia]]''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Salvia sclarea (Clary Sage, Clear Eye, Europe Sage, Eyebright) {{!}} North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox |url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/salvia-sclarea/ |access-date=2022-05-20 |website=plants.ces.ncsu.edu}}</ref> It is native to the northern [[Mediterranean Basin]] and to some areas in [[north Africa]] and [[Central Asia]].{{cn|date=May 2022}} The plant has long been cultivated as an herb and is currently grown for its [[essential oil]].<ref name="Clebsch">{{cite book|last1=Clebsch|first1=Betsy|last2=Barner|first2=Carol D.|title=The New Book of Salvias|publisher=Timber Press|year=2003|page=261|isbn=978-0-88192-560-9|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NM0iwB8GrQYC&pg=PA261}}</ref>

==Description==
''Salvia sclarea'' reaches {{convert|3|to|4|ft|m|abbr=on}} in height, with thick, square stems covered in hairs. The leaves are approximately {{convert|1|ft|m|abbr=on}} long at the base, and {{convert|.5|ft|m|abbr=on}} long higher up on the plant. The upper leaf surface is rugose, and covered with glandular hairs. The flowers are in verticils, with between two and six flowers in each verticil, and are held in large colorful bracts that range in color from pale mauve to lilac or white-to-pink with a pink mark on the edge. The lilac or pale-blue corolla is approximately {{convert|1|in|cm|abbr=on}}, with the lips held wide open.<ref name="Clebsch" /> The cultivar ''S. sclarea'' 'Turkestanica' bears pink stems, petiolate leaves, and white, pink-flecked blossoms on spikes that grow up to {{convert|30|in|cm}} tall.<ref>{{cite book | author = Mark Griffiths | title = Index of Garden Plants | edition = 2nd American | location = Portland, Oregon | publisher = Timber Press | date = 1995 | isbn = 0-88192-246-3 }}.</ref>

==History==
The plant’s medicinal uses are described as far back as the 4th century BCE, in the writings of [[Theophrastus]], as well as in the 1st century CE writings of [[Dioscorides]] and [[Pliny the Elder]]).<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wagner |first1=Charles |last2=De Gezelle |first2=Jillian |last3=Komarnytsky |first3=Slavko |date=2020-02-28 |title=Celtic Provenance in Traditional Herbal Medicine of Medieval Wales and Classical Antiquity |journal=Frontiers in Pharmacology |volume=11 |pages=105 |doi=10.3389/fphar.2020.00105 |issn=1663-9812 |pmc=7058801 |pmid=32184721|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Clary seeds have a [[Mucilage|mucilaginous]] coat, which is why some centuries-old herbal guides recommend placing a seed into the eye of someone with a foreign object in it so that it could adhere to the object and make it easy to remove. This practice is noted by [[Nicholas Culpeper]] in his ''Complete Herbal'' (1653), who referred to the plant as "clear-eye".<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.bibliomania.com/2/1/66/113/20994/1/frameset.html | title = ''The Complete Herbal'': Clary, or More Properly Clear-Eye | website = bibliomania.com }}</ref>

It has also long been used as an additive to [[wine]] and [[beer]]. In 16th-century Germany [[elderflower]]-infused clary was added to [[Rhine wine]]s to make a more potent beverage known as [[Muscatel]].<ref name=rodale>{{cite book | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=htGD3Y7WNxwC | title = Rodale's Illustrated Encyclopedia of Herbs | isbn = 978-0-87596-964-0 | last1 = Kowalchik | first1 = Claire | last2 = Hylton | first2 = William H. | date = 15 January 1998 | publisher = Rodale }}</ref>

==Uses==
[[File:Winton Township field on NC 461.jpg|thumb|Cultivated field in northeastern [[North Carolina]]]]

The distilled [[essential oil]] of ''Salvia sclarea'' is used widely in [[perfume]]s (most often as a supporting note<ref>{{Cite web |title=Мускатный шалфей: растение с историей и характером |url=https://muscatshalfei.ru/ |access-date=2025-12-26 |website=muscatshalfei.ru}}</ref>) and as a muscatel-like flavoring for [[vermouth]]s, wines, and [[liqueur]]s.<ref name="Clebsch" /> The aroma is described as "fresh, herbal, tea, weedy, dry, sage, spicy".<ref>{{cite web |title=salvia sclarea oil|url=https://scentsandflavors.com/database/9dbb4b12-ca89-4e00-93d2-4c18d1365592|website=Scents and Flavors |publisher=Scents and Flavors |access-date=4 April 2026}}</ref> It is also used in [[aromatherapy]].<ref name="Kintzios">{{cite book|last=Kintzios|first=Spiridon E.|title=Sage: The Genus Salvia|publisher=CRC Press|year=2000|page=20|isbn=978-90-5823-005-8|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=iE7-nuI9S7UC&pg=PA20}}</ref>

In the [[United States]], this oil is mostly produced on a large scale in and around [[Bertie County, North Carolina|Bertie County]] in northeastern [[North Carolina]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Leffingwell |first1=John C. |last2=Stallings |first2=John W. | last3=Sellers | first3=Franklin O.| last4=Lloyd | first4=Robert A. | last5=Kane Jr. | first5=Franklin C.|name-list-style=amp |date=1974 |title=Clary Sage Production in the Southeastern United States |journal=6th International Congress of Essential Oils }}</ref>
